verses.text: Now these are the words of the letter that Jeremiah the prophet sent from Jerusalem to the residue of the elders of the captivity, and to the priests, to the prophets, and to all the people, whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away captive from Jerusalem to Babylon,
(after that Jeconiah the king, the queen mother, the eunuchs, the princes of Judah and Jerusalem, the craftsmen, and the smiths, had departed from Jerusalem),
by the hand of Elasah the son of Shaphan, and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, (whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to Babylon to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon), saying,
Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says to all the captivity, whom I have caused to be carried away captive from Jerusalem to Babylon:
“Build houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat their fruit.
Take wives, and father sons and daughters; and take wives for your sons, and give your daughters to husbands, that they may bear sons and daughters; and multiply there, and don’t be diminished.
Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to Yahweh for it; for in its peace you shall have peace.”
For Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel says: “Don’t let your prophets who are among you, and your diviners, deceive you; neither listen to your dreams which you cause to be dreamed.
For they prophesy falsely to you in my name. I have not sent them,” says Yahweh.
For Yahweh says, “After seventy years are accomplished for Babylon, I will visit you, and perform my good word toward you, in causing you to return to this place.
For I know the thoughts that I think toward you,” says Yahweh, “thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you hope and a future.
You shall call on me, and you shall go and pray to me, and I will listen to you.
You shall seek me, and find me, when you shall search for me with all your heart.

I will be found by you,” says Yahweh, “and I will turn again your captivity, and I will gather you from all the nations, and from all the places where I have driven you, says Yahweh; and I will bring you again to the place from where I caused you to be carried away captive.”
Because you have said, “Yahweh has raised us up prophets in Babylon;”
Yahweh says concerning the king who sits on David’s throne, and concerning all the people who dwell in this city, your brothers who haven’t gone with you into captivity;
Yahweh of Armies says: “Behold, I will send on them the sword, the famine, and the pestilence, and will make them like vile figs, that can’t be eaten, they are so bad.

I will pursue after them with the sword, with the famine, and with the pestilence, and will deliver them to be tossed back and forth among all the kingdoms of the earth, to be an object of horror, and an astonishment, and a hissing, and a reproach, among all the nations where I have driven them;
because they have not listened to my words,” says Yahweh, “with which I sent to them my servants the prophets, rising up early and sending them; but you would not hear,” says Yahweh.
Hear therefore Yahweh’s word, all you of the captivity, whom I have sent away from Jerusalem to Babylon.

Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says concerning Ahab the son of Kolaiah, and concerning Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, who prophesy a lie to you in my name: “Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon; and he shall kill them before your eyes.
A curse shall be taken up about them by all the captives of Judah who are in Babylon, saying, ‘Yahweh make you like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire;’

because they have done foolish things in Israel, and have committed adultery with their neighbors’ wives, and have spoken words in my name falsely, which I didn’t command them. I am he who knows, and am witness,” says Yahweh.
Concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite you shall speak, saying,

“Thus speaks Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, saying, ‘Because you have sent letters in your own name to all the people who are at Jerusalem, and to Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah, the priest, and to all the priests, saying,

“Yahweh has made you priest in the place of Jehoiada the priest, that there may be officers in Yahweh’s house, for every man who is mad, and makes himself a prophet, that you should put him in the stocks and in shackles.
Now therefore, why have you not rebuked Jeremiah of Anathoth, who makes himself a prophet to you,
because he has sent to us in Babylon, saying, The captivity is long: build houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat their fruit?”’”
Zephaniah the priest read this letter in the ears of Jeremiah the prophet.
Then Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah, saying,
“Send to all them of the captivity, saying, ‘Yahweh says concerning Shemaiah the Nehelamite: “Because Shemaiah has prophesied to you, and I didn’t send him, and he has caused you to trust in a lie;”

therefore Yahweh says, “Behold, I will punish Shemaiah the Nehelamite, and his offspring.  He shall not have a man to dwell among this people, neither shall he see the good that I will do to my people,” says Yahweh, “because he has spoken rebellion against Yahweh.”’”

footnotes.content: A letter sent to exiles—those carried far from home. Jeremiah doesn't hesitate to reach them where they are, speaking truth across the distance. The Lord's shepherd searches for his scattered sheep, and his word finds them in Babylon just as surely as in Jerusalem.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even kings and craftsmen, the powerful and the skilled—all are captive. No one is exempt from exile's hard reality. Yet this very humbling levels us all before God, reminding us that our standing before Him has nothing to do with earthly rank or usefulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elasah and Gemariah carry Jeremiah's letter—ordinary men chosen for an extraordinary errand. The Lord often uses the faithful few to carry His Word where it must go. Two men, one scroll, and through them His comfort reaches thousands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Yahweh of Armies"—the God who commands all creation speaks directly to captives. He doesn't hide His face from those in exile; He owns their captivity and speaks to them in it. That is the beginning of all comfort.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Build houses. Plant gardens. Eat fruit. The exiles might have expected a call to rage or despair, but God calls them to ordinary faithfulness—to settle, to work, to nourish themselves in a strange land. Sometimes the most faithful thing is to live well where you've been placed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Marry. Have children. Seek grandchildren. In captivity, God calls them toward the future, toward life multiplying and continuing. He is saying: your story does not end in exile; it continues through your children and theirs. Hope is not foolish—it is godly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seek the peace of the city. Pray for your captors. This cuts against everything our grieving hearts want—yet it is the path to our own peace. When we bless the place where we suffer, we release the bitterness that would destroy us. The Lord's peace flows through our intercession.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: False prophets whisper in Babylon too—seductive dreams, convenient words. The enemy works the same lies in exile as at home. God warns His people to test every voice, every dream, against His steadfast truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I have not sent them." God's signature is His honesty. False prophets come in His name but claim commission He never gave. The true prophet always points back to God's actual Word, never beyond it or around it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seventy years—a long exile, yet finite. God has set a limit and a promise: He will return His people home. For captives in despair, knowing the captivity has an end is itself a gift. The Lord's purposes cannot be thwarted forever.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Thoughts of peace, not evil." I have learned, through much sorrow, that God's intentions toward us are always good, even in seasons when the path looks like ruin. He knows what He is about, and His plans will outlast our pain.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Call on Him. Pray to Him. He will listen. This is the standing invitation—not when you are pure, not when the moment is perfect, but now, in your captivity, in your confusion. Prayer itself is the open door.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seek with all your heart. Not half-hearted glancing, but the deep seeking of one who has lost what matters most. When we search for God as a refugee searches for home, we find Him—because He has never left us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "I will be found." God promises not just abstract presence but encounter—the warmth of finding what has been lost. He will gather the scattered and bring them home. The exile does not last forever; the homecoming is sure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The exiles have claimed prophets in Babylon—false comfort, false hope. They want their ears tickled, their captivity justified or minimized. But Jeremiah's true word speaks harder truths that lead, paradoxically, to real hope.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Those who stayed behind in Jerusalem will suffer differently from those in exile. The city itself will fall. God's judgment reaches everywhere—there is no refuge except in Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Vile figs, inedible—a picture from the marketplace that any farmer would understand. God's judgment is often described in images we know: spoiled grain, withered vines, rotted fruit. He speaks in our language about real consequences.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pursuit with sword, famine, pestilence—the full weight of God's justice falls on those who ignore His Word. They will be tossed among nations, objects of horror and scorn. This is the cost of hardening against God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "My servants the prophets, rising up early and sending them." God's patience is visible—He rose early to send His messengers, again and again. But His patience, though long, is not infinite; there comes a point when judgment follows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Hear therefore Yahweh's word." After the pronouncement of judgment on those who stayed, the exiles are called to hear and distinguish themselves through obedience. To hear and receive the true word is itself survival.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahab and Zedekiah—named liars in Babylon. Judgment often works through exposure: the false prophets are identified, their deception laid bare before all. To contradict God's Word always ends in shame.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Their names become a curse—"make you like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king roasted." To live in defiance of God is to become a warning to others. What a terrible legacy for a prophet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Adultery, false words spoken in God's name—their sins blend the personal betrayal with the spiritual lie. Both pollute. Both invite judgment. Yet God knows and witnesses; nothing escapes His eye.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shemaiah the Nehelamite steps into view—another false prophet, sending letters, stirring up dissent. Falsehood loves company and spreads through writing and rumor. God addresses this conspiracy directly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shemaiah sends letters in his own name, addressing the priest Zephaniah. False prophets work through networks, building alliances among the respected and powerful. They move by human influence, not God's Spirit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priest is given authority to lock up mad prophets. But Shemaiah uses this authority corruptly—turning it into a weapon to silence true messengers. Institutional power, twisted by vanity, becomes persecution.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Why have you not rebuked Jeremiah?" The pressure mounts—powerful voices aligned against the true prophet. Yet Jeremiah stands firm. God does not withdraw His messengers when opposition grows; He sustains them through it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shemaiah quotes Jeremiah's own words—build houses, plant gardens—and uses them to discredit him. False prophets often twist truth just enough to poison it. They distort what is good to make it sound naive.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zephaniah reads Shemaiah's letter aloud in Jeremiah's hearing. The priest becomes an unwitting messenger of opposition. Yet this public confrontation brings the conflict into light where truth can be tested.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then Yahweh's word came to Jeremiah. In the moment of pressure, when the conspiracy is made known, God speaks again to His prophet. His Word is not withdrawn; it flows toward the faithful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shemaiah prophesied without commission; he made people trust a lie. God judges not just the content of false prophecy but the trust it corrupts. To lead someone into deception is to wound their very soul.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: No son to dwell among the people. He will not see the good the Lord brings His people. The false prophet forfeits both future and family, legacy and promise. To oppose God's Word is to oppose one's own flourishing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
